note: Abstract: accuracy swings from near chance to near SOTA with prompt format, example choice and order; attributed to bias toward answers late in the prompt or common in pretraining data. Matches the entry's supports. Note: the record's extra statements (effects persist across model sizes; bias toward labels frequent in the examples) are not stated in the abstract, so this source covers only the abstract-level claim.

Page states load/batch-size variation without batch invariance is the primary cause, and floating-point non-associativity is the underlying mechanism. Page also says concurrency/atomic adds are uninvolved; the record's wording (reduction order depends on kernel choice, batch size) is consistent.

Abstract: LLM-integrated apps blur the line between data and instructions; injected prompts in retrieved data can control 'how and if other APIs are called'. Matches the record's 'how and whether' sentence.
Abstract introduces pass^k and reports gpt-4o succeeding on <50% of tasks and pass^8 <25% in retail, so repeated-trial reliability is far below single-run success.
Abstract covers position, verbosity, self-enhancement biases and over 80% agreement of strong judges (GPT-4) with human preferences.

Abstract: LIMA fine-tuned on 1,000 curated prompt-response pairs; authors conclude almost all knowledge is learned in pretraining and limited instruction-tuning data suffices. Supports the entry as worded.

Abstract: LoRA underperforms full finetuning in standard low-rank settings on code/math, but maintains base-model performance outside the target domain and forgets less than weight decay/dropout. Matches the record's sentence.
Abstract: frozen pretrained weights, trainable low-rank matrices in each layer, large reduction in trainable parameters, no extra inference latency vs adapters.
Abstract: instructions planted in data likely to be retrieved; applications blur data/instructions; effective defenses lacking at the time. Supports the Greshake sentence in the record.
Abstract: iterative correct-and-re-embed recovers 92% of 32-token inputs exactly; full names recovered from clinical notes. Supports 'embeddings can leak information about the source text'.

SmoothQuant abstract frames the method as moving activation-outlier difficulty onto weights because weights are easy to quantise and activations are not. A later targeted re-check of the exact phrase was blocked by a session limit, so the exact wording is judged from the earlier fetch summary. Supports the record's outlier/activation claim.

Abstract: hallucinations tied to binary-classification-style errors under statistical pressures; models optimised as test-takers; benchmarks reward guessing over admitting uncertainty; proposes changing scoring of existing benchmarks.

Larger models are well calibrated on multiple-choice/true-false with the right format, and P(True) works well and improves with several samples. But the abstract's 'struggles on new tasks' caveat applies to the P(IK) predictor (partial cross-task transfer), not to P(True) self-rating. The record attaches the new-task caveat to the rating of the model's own answer.
narrowed_supports: Larger models give reasonably reliable confidence estimates on multiple-choice and true/false tasks when the format is right; asking a model to propose an answer then rate its probability of being correct works fairly well and improves with several samples; the related P(IK) predictor (does the model know the answer) transfers only partly and calibrates poorly on new tasks.
